# Results — Study 41 (Hangover): the January Barometer on the S&P 500, 1950–2025

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly **price return** of the **S&P 500
(^GSPC)** — no dividends: ^GSPC is a price index and the total-return ^SP500TR only starts in 1988 —
daily from Yahoo resampled to month-end, 1950–2025 (**76 years**). Cash years credited the 13-week
T-bill (^IRX; zero pre-1960, before the tape starts). The omen: sign(January) predicts
sign(rest-of-year). As-of **2026-05-31**; inputs fingerprint `fed7f700c91b`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `WEAK` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Predicts the year"? `NOT SUPPORTED`

The January Barometer's *directional* claim — as goes January, so goes the year — is `NOT SUPPORTED`
against the only honest benchmark, the **base rate**. The rest of the year is up **76%** of the time
*unconditionally* (stocks just rise); the omen's directional accuracy is **68%** — it is **beaten by a
constant that always predicts "up"**. There is a `WEAK` real residue, and it survives the small-sample
tests: a *down* January does precede a softer rest-of-year (**+2.1%, up 60%** vs **+12.2%, up 87%**;
Fisher exact **p = 0.012** on the proportions, permutation **p = 0.002** on the mean gap). But that's
`MIRAGE` tradability: sitting in T-bills after a down January cuts drawdown (−40% → −16%) only by
**reducing equity exposure** — a permanently smaller stock weight does the same — it acts once a year,
and its CAGR edge on this tape is a **price-only artefact** (dividends, which the tape omits, accrue
to buy-and-hold every year but to the omen only when invested).

## Data stamp

- **Index**: S&P 500 (^GSPC) monthly **price return** (no dividends), 1950 → 2025, 76 years
- **Cash leg**: 13-week T-bill (^IRX) monthly yield, 1960 → 2025; the three 1950s cash years earn zero
- As-of **2026-05-31** (in-progress months dropped); inputs fingerprint `fed7f700c91b`

## The omen vs the base rate

| | n | rest-of-year mean | P(rest-of-year up) | Wilson 95% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| after an **up** January | 46 | **+12.2%** | 87% | [74%, 94%] |
| after a **down** January | 30 | **+2.1%** | 60% | [42%, 75%] |
| **unconditional** (the base rate) | 76 | +8.2% | **76%** | [66%, 84%] |

> Up-vs-down January split: **Fisher exact p = 0.012** on P(up), and the **+10.2 pp** rest-of-year
> mean gap survives a seeded 20,000-shuffle permutation test (**p = 0.002**). The conditioning is
> real — that is the `WEAK` residue. Note the small-n honesty, though: the down-January cell *on its
> own* (60%, Wilson [42%, 75%]) cannot be told apart from the 76% base rate; what's detectable is the
> up-vs-down *contrast*.

> Directional accuracy of the omen: **68.4%** (Wilson [57%, 78%]) — *below* the 76.3% (Wilson
> [66%, 84%]) you get by always predicting "up". As a *predictor*, the barometer is worse than
> ignoring January entirely.

The believers' headline ("the rest of the year is up 87% after an up January!") is a **base-rate
illusion**: the rest of the year is up most of the time *regardless*. The only informative cell is the
down-January one — and even there the market still rises on average.

## The tradable version vs just holding the index

| (rest-of-year only, price-only tape) | CAGR | annual Sharpe | max-DD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Buy & hold (Feb–Dec, every year) | +7.2% | 0.57 | −40% |
| Barometer (T-bill after a down January) | **+8.3%** | **0.87** | **−16%** |

With the cash years finally credited the T-bill (the earlier draft paid them zero), the rule's
risk-adjusted edge is real *on this tape* — but read the tape's label. **It's price-only.** Dividends
ran ~3–4%/yr over the sample and accrue to buy-and-hold in **all 76 years** but to the barometer only
in its **46 invested years**: crediting them would hand buy-and-hold roughly an extra ~1.4%/yr
relative to the rule — about the entire CAGR gap. What genuinely survives is the shallower drawdown,
and that is bought the boring way: by being **out of the market** in ~40% of years. It isn't timing;
it's holding less equity. A static lower-equity weight (plus T-bills) buys the same risk reduction
without the calendar story.

## The decay story, retold honestly

| | directional accuracy | Wilson 95% | down-January rest-of-year |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1950–1972 (before Hirsch named it) | 78% (18/23) | [58%, 90%] | −0.4% |
| 1973–2025 (after) | 64% (34/53) | [51%, 76%] | +3.0% |

The point estimates *look* like post-publication decay — sharper before the omen was famous, fainter
after. But the subsamples are 23 and 53 years: **Fisher exact p = 0.29** on the accuracy difference,
and the two Wilson intervals overlap almost entirely. The honest reading is that the data are
*consistent with* some decay and equally consistent with none — on samples this small the
post-publication-fade story cannot be established, only not ruled out.

## The honest takeaway

The January Barometer is **not a forecaster** — as a directional omen it loses to "stocks go up". Its
one measurable residue (a down January precedes a weaker year) is small but real — it survives Fisher
and permutation tests (p = 0.012 / 0.002) — yet it "trades" only by cutting equity exposure once a
year, its CAGR edge evaporates on a total-return tape, and any post-1972 decay is statistically
indistinguishable from noise either way. `WEAK` signal, `MIRAGE` tradability, `NOT SUPPORTED` as the
year-ahead barometer it's sold as.
